reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A position is sold off in equal parts over $T = 8$ trading days. Liquidity-adjusted VaR is the 1-day VaR times $\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$.
ask: The percentage by which LVaR exceeds the 1-day VaR is closest to:

options.why: Took the factor minus one, 0.785, and read it as 0.785% instead of 78.5%.
Forgot the square root: $9\times17/48 = 3.19$, an increase of 219%.
Scaled the VaR by $T$ itself (8 times the 1-day figure), an increase of 700%.

takeaway: The liquidation factor is a square root, so 8 days adds under 80%, nowhere near 8 times.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: Equity position of USD 1,000,000 with annual volatility 34.0%. Assume 250 trading days a year, i.i.d. normal returns and a 99% quantile of 2.33. The first step of the LVaR chain is the plain 1-day 99% VaR.
ask: The 1-day 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: About USD 790,000
options.why: Used the annual volatility directly, with no scaling down to one day: $1{,}000{,}000\times0.34\times2.33$.

options.label: About USD 3,200
options.why: Divided the annual volatility by 250 instead of by $\sqrt{250}$.

takeaway: Annual to daily volatility divides by $\sqrt{250}\approx 15.8$, not by 250.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A share trades at a midprice of USD 50.00 with a bid-ask spread of USD 0.35. The relative spread has a standard deviation of 0.20% (0.0020). The 99% transactions cost per share is the half-spread plus its spread risk: $P\times\tfrac12(s + 2.33\,\sigma_s)$.
ask: Which part of the 99% cost per share is larger?

options.label: The spread-risk add-on
options.why: Dropped the $\tfrac12$ on the risk term: $2.33\times0.0020\times50 = 0.233$ would beat 0.175, but with the $\tfrac12$ it is only 0.1165.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: The two pieces sit in the same range but not at the same value: 0.175 against 0.1165.

takeaway: In the transactions-cost formula the half-spread is the bulk, with the 99% spread risk adding a smaller top-up.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A position with a 1-day VaR of USD 62 million is liquidated in equal parts over $T = 4$ trading days. LVaR $=$ VaR$_{1\text{-day}}\times\sqrt{(1+T)(1+2T)/(6T)}$. Plain square-root-of-time scaling over 4 days would give $62\times\sqrt{4} = $ USD 124 million.
ask: Compared with USD 124 million, the LVaR is:

options.label: Equal
options.why: Treated the liquidation factor as $\sqrt{T} = 2$. The actual factor is $\sqrt{45/24} = 1.37$.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Assumed the sell-down adds risk on top of $\sqrt{T}$ scaling. The position shrinks as it is sold, so average exposure is smaller.

takeaway: The sell-down ramp makes LVaR grow more slowly than $\sqrt{T}$ scaling: the position shrinks while it is sold.

reading: LTR-2: Liquidity and Leverage
setup: A share is priced at USD 50.00 with a bid-ask spread of USD 0.350. The relative spread $s$ has a volatility of 20 basis points (0.20%). The 99% transactions cost per share is $P\times\tfrac12(s + 2.33\,\sigma_s)$.
ask: The 99% transactions cost per share is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.006
options.why: Stopped at the relative cost $0.00583$ and never multiplied by the USD 50 price.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.03
options.why: Scale slip (1/10): lost a decimal place in the final multiplication.

options.label: ≈ USD 11.8
options.why: Entered $\sigma_s$ as 0.20 (a 20% spread volatility) instead of 0.0020.

takeaway: Convert basis points to decimals before plugging in, and remember the cost is per share: multiply by the price.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A Treasury bill with face value USD 100 is bought for USD 88 and matures in 120 days. Bank discount rate: $\frac{F-P}{F}\times\frac{360}{t}$. Bond-equivalent yield: $\frac{F-P}{P}\times\frac{365}{t}$.
ask: For this bill, the bond-equivalent yield is:

options.label: Lower than the discount rate
options.why: Thought the discount rate, quoted on the bigger-looking face value, must be the larger. It divides by the larger base (100, not 88) and uses the shorter 360-day year, so it understates the yield.

options.label: Equal to the discount rate
options.why: Treated both as the same annualised return. They use different bases (face against price) and different year lengths (360 against 365).

takeaway: Discount rate divides by face and uses 360 days; both choices make it lower than the yield on price.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A Treasury bill is priced at USD 89.84 per USD 100 face and matures in 124 days. The bank discount rate uses face value as the base and a 360-day year.
ask: The bank discount rate is closest to:

options.why: Inverted the annualisation: $0.1016\times124/360$ instead of $\times360/124$.
Stopped at the 124-day discount of 10.16 per 100 and never annualised it.
Scale slip (10×): misplaced the decimal after annualising.

takeaway: Annualise by scaling up: $360/t$ is a number above 1 for any bill under a year.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A money-market security is priced at USD 95 per USD 100 face, with 85 days to maturity (360-day year). The same data sheet lists a required rate of return of 12% and a yield to maturity of 8%.
ask: The bank discount rate is closest to:

options.label: About 12%
options.why: Lifted the required rate of return off the data sheet. It is not an input to a discount rate.

options.label: About 8%
options.why: Lifted the stated yield to maturity. The discount rate is computed from price, face and days.

options.label: About 5%
options.why: Stopped at the USD 5 raw discount and never annualised it by 360/85.

takeaway: A discount rate comes from price, face value and days. Other rates quoted alongside are distractors.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bond with par USD 1,500 pays a 10% annual coupon (USD 150) and matures in 4 years. It trades at USD 1,200. Its current yield is $150/1{,}200 = 12.5\%$.
ask: The yield to maturity is:

options.label: Equal to 12.5%
options.why: Treated the coupon over price as the whole return. The bond also gains USD 300 as it pulls up to par.

options.label: Below 12.5%
options.why: Anchored on the 10% coupon rate and pulled the figure down. A bond below par earns its coupon plus the pull to par.

takeaway: A bond bought below par has YTM above its current yield, which is above its coupon rate.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bond with par USD 2,000 pays an 8% annual coupon (USD 160), matures in 5 years and trades at USD 1,600. A quick estimate of yield is (annual coupon + annual pull to par) divided by the average of price and par.
ask: That estimate is closest to:

options.label: About 10%
options.why: Used the current yield $160/1{,}600$ only, ignoring the USD 400 pull to par.

options.label: About 8%
options.why: Used the coupon rate, which ignores both the discount price and the pull to par.

takeaway: For a discount bond: coupon rate < current yield < YTM.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A taxed financial firm in the 35% federal bracket holds an Aaa municipal bond with a 5% gross yield to maturity, which is tax-exempt. The tax-equivalent yield is the tax-exempt yield divided by $(1 - t)$.
ask: The taxable bond that gives the same after-tax return must yield:

options.label: Less than 5%
options.why: Multiplied by $(1-t) = 0.65$, getting 3.25%, as if the municipal bond were the taxed one.

options.label: Exactly 5%
options.why: Ignored the 35% tax on the taxable bond. A 5% taxable bond would leave only 3.25% after tax.

takeaway: Tax-equivalent yield is always above the muni yield: divide by $(1-t)$, never multiply.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bank holds a municipal bond with a 5% tax-exempt return, funded at a pretax cost of 3.7%. The tax rate is 40%, and only 75% of the interest expense is deductible. Net after-tax return is the 1.30% gross spread plus the tax shield on deductible interest.
ask: Compared with the 1.30% gross spread, the net after-tax return is:

options.label: Equal to 1.30%
options.why: Left out the tax shield. The deductible part of the funding cost reduces the bank's taxes and adds to the return.

options.label: Below 1.30%
options.why: Taxed the spread at 40% ($1.30\times0.60 = 0.78\%$). The municipal interest itself is exempt.

takeaway: On a bank-qualified muni the funding cost partly shields tax, so the net return is above the pretax spread.

reading: LTR-4: The Investment Function in Financial-Services Management
setup: A bank buys a bank-qualified municipal bond with a 5.5% tax-exempt return, funded at 4.7%. The marginal tax rate is 34%, and 80% of the interest expense is deductible. Net after-tax return is the gross spread plus the tax shield on the deductible interest.
ask: The net after-tax return is closest to:

options.why: Taxed the 0.80% spread at 34% and called the tax the return.
Stopped at the gross spread and left out the tax shield on the deductible interest.
Quoted the bond's own return and ignored the funding cost.

takeaway: The deductible funding cost is worth more than the spread itself here: shield 1.28% against spread 0.80%.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Mountain Top Savings projects a net liquidity deficit of USD 10m next week. Supplies (USD m): deposit inflows 26, nondeposit revenue 18, customer loan repayments 23, asset sales 10, money market borrowings 15. Demands other than deposit withdrawals: quality loans 32, repayment of borrowings 15, dividends 10, operating expenses 15.
ask: The deposit withdrawals needed to produce the −10 position are:

options.label: USD 20m
options.why: Stopped at supply minus the other demands (92 − 72 = 20), which would give a balanced position, not a deficit.

options.label: USD 10m
options.why: Read the −10 deficit as the withdrawal figure itself.

takeaway: Net position $=$ supply $-$ demand: withdrawals must exceed the pre-withdrawal surplus by the size of the deficit.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: ABC Bank forecasts next-day cash flows (USD m). Inflows: deposit inflows 119, money market borrowings 110, asset sales 61, nondeposit-services revenue 118, scheduled loan repayments 122. Outflows: deposit withdrawals 129, acceptable loan requests 90, stockholder dividends 172, repayment of bank borrowings 84, operating expenses 70.
ask: The projected net liquidity position is a:

options.label: Surplus
options.why: Left the USD 172m dividend out of the demands, giving $530 - 373 = +157$.

options.label: Exact balance
options.why: Treated 530 against 545 as close enough to net out. The gap is USD 15m of outflows with no source.

takeaway: Add every inflow and every outflow, dividends included. A small gap can still be a deficit.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Greenlux State Bank, next 24 hours (USD m): incoming deposits 90, customer loan repayments 25, asset sales 20, nondeposit fee income 15; deposit withdrawals 60, acceptable loan requests 45, repayment of the bank's own borrowings 5.
ask: The projected net liquidity position is a:

options.label: Deficit
options.why: Counted both 'repayment' items as outflows. Customer loan repayments are a source of liquidity; only repaying the bank's own borrowings is a use: $125 - 135 = -10$.

takeaway: Repayments of loans owed to the bank are a source; repayments of borrowings the bank owes are a use.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Grand Bank's liquidity manager sees four scenarios for next month's liquidity position (USD m), with probabilities: 45% at −500, 20% at −575, 25% at +350, 10% at +100.
ask: Compared with the simple average of the four outcomes (−156.25), the expected (probability-weighted) position is:

options.label: A smaller deficit
options.why: Weighted the surplus scenarios too heavily. They carry only 35% of the probability, against 65% for the two deficit scenarios.

options.label: The same
options.why: Used equal weights of 25%, which is what the simple average does.

takeaway: Expected value uses the probabilities: here the likelier deficit cases pull it below the plain average.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Daylight Bank (USD m): federal funds sold and reverse repos 396; federal funds purchased and repurchase agreements 488; total assets 3,431. Other balance-sheet items are not needed. Net fed funds and repo position $=$ (sold − purchased) / total assets.
ask: The net position is:

options.label: Positive, a net lender
options.why: Subtracted in the wrong order (purchased minus sold), giving +2.68%.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Treated the two lines as offsetting. They differ by USD 92m.

takeaway: Sold minus purchased: a negative net position means the bank is a net borrower in the fed funds and repo market.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Daylight Bank (USD m): cash and due from depository institutions 546; US Treasuries 382; other securities 550; pledged securities 503; fed funds sold and reverse repos 396; net loans 2,374; total assets 3,431; total deposits 2,686; core deposits 1,111. The cash position indicator is cash and due from depository institutions divided by total assets.
ask: The indicator is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (1/10): misplaced the decimal when converting to a percent.
Divided by core deposits (1,111) instead of total assets.
Scale slip (10×): misplaced the decimal when converting to a percent.

takeaway: Check the denominator: the cash position indicator is measured against total assets, and a cash ratio above 100% should always ring an alarm.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: Kingstreet Savings, vulnerable funds (USD m): checkable deposits 20, savings deposits 40, nonpersonal time deposits 70. The legal reserve is 10% on checkable and savings deposits and 0% on nonpersonal time deposits. The 50% desired reserve is applied to funds net of legal reserves.
ask: The legal reserves held against the vulnerable funds are:

options.label: USD 13.0m
options.why: Applied the 10% to all 130 including time deposits, which carry a 0% requirement.

options.label: USD 2.0m
options.why: Applied 10% to checkable deposits only and left out savings deposits.

takeaway: Legal reserves apply only to the categories that carry a requirement, and are deducted before the desired percentage.

reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
setup: A bank's liabilities (USD m, desired reserve): hot money 50 at 80%, vulnerable funds 55 at 30%, core funds 100 at 20%. Legal reserves are 3% of each category, and the desired percentages apply after deducting them. Loans are 165 and could reach 225, a 60 loan requirement that is not part of the liability reserve.
ask: The liability liquidity reserve is:

options.label: Equal to USD 76.5m
options.why: Applied the desired percentages to the gross balances ($40+16.5+20 = 76.5$) and skipped the 3% legal-reserve deduction.

options.label: Above USD 130m
options.why: Added the USD 60m loan requirement, which belongs to the total liquidity requirement, not the liability reserve.

takeaway: Net the legal reserves first: the liability reserve is slightly below the gross figure, and loans are added only for the total requirement.
